Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be positive real numbers with $\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} + \sqrt{c} = \frac12\cdot\sqrt{3}$. Prove that the system of equations
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{y-a} + \sqrt{z-a} &= 1 &(1)\\ \sqrt{z-b} + \sqrt{x-b} &= 1 &(2)\\ \sqrt{x-c} + \sqrt{y-c} &= 1 &(3) \end{aligned}$$
has exactly one solution $(x, y, z)$ with real numbers $x, y, z$.

Prove: if the lengths of the edges of a tetrahedron $ABCD$ are not smaller than $\sqrt{3}$ and not greater than $2$, then the interior angles between any two faces of the tetrahedron $ABCD$ are not greater than $90^\circ$.

(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Investigate whether there are $40$ consecutive natural numbers which are all smaller than $10^9$ and not primes.

Version B. Determine all those positive real numbers $k$ for which the sequence $(x_n)$ defined by
$$x_1 = 1, \qquad x_{n+1} = \sqrt{k\left(x_n^2 + x_n\right)} \quad (n = 1, 2, 3, \dots)$$
is convergent. For each such number $k$, determine the limit of the sequence $(x_n)$.

Five guests come to a party. The host notices that among any three of these guests there are always two who know each other and two who do not know each other. Prove that the host can seat his five guests at a round table in such a way that on both sides of each guest sit acquaintances of this guest.

Let $q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n$ ($n \ge 2$) be pairwise distinct primes. Prove that this assumption always implies
$$\frac{q_1^3 + 1}{q_1^3 - 1}\cdot\frac{q_2^3 + 1}{q_2^3 - 1}\cdot\ldots\cdot\frac{q_n^3 + 1}{q_n^3 - 1} < \frac{36}{25}.$$

Is there a function $f$ which is defined for all real numbers, has real function values and satisfies the following conditions (1), (2)?
(1) For all real numbers $x$ and $y$: $f(x+y) = \dfrac{f(x) + f(y)}{1 + f(x)f(y)}$.
(2) $f(1) = \frac12$.

Let $A_1A_2A_3A_4$ be a tetrahedron with given edge lengths $\overline{A_1A_2} = a$, $\overline{A_1A_3} = b$, $\overline{A_1A_4} = c$, $\overline{A_2A_3} = d$, $\overline{A_2A_4} = e$, $\overline{A_3A_4} = f$. Investigate whether there is a point $P$ in space such that the sum $s$ of the squares of the distances of the point $P$ from the vertices of the tetrahedron attains a smallest value. If so, determine this smallest value of $s$ for given $a, b, c, d, e, f$.

Let $(p_n)$ be the sequence of primes ordered by size, i.e.
$$p_1 = 2, \quad p_2 = 3, \quad p_3 = 5, \quad p_4 = 7, \quad \dots$$
Investigate whether there is a natural number $N$ such that for all natural numbers $n$ with $n > N$ the inequality $p_n > 4n$ holds.

(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. A natural number represented in the decimal system is called a mirror number if its digits are arranged symmetrically, i.e. if the first and the last, the second and the second-to-last, etc. digits coincide. For example, the numbers $358853$, $27672$, $44444$ are mirror numbers. Investigate whether for every two-digit natural number $a$ whose last digit is different from $0$ there is a mirror number different from $0$ which is divisible by $a$.

Version B. For every triangle $ABC$, let $d$ denote the length of the diameter of the incircle, $g$ the largest side length and $\varepsilon$ the size of the smallest angle of the triangle $ABC$.
(a) Prove: there is a constant $K$ such that for every triangle $ABC$ the following inequality (1) holds:
$$\frac1d < \frac{K}{g\sin\varepsilon}. \qquad (1)$$
(b) Among all constants $K$ for which the statement to be proved in (a) holds, determine the smallest constant, if it exists.

$500$ candies are to be packed into a joke parcel, using wrappings of suitable sizes, in such a way that the following conditions (1), (2) are satisfied. Here (2) refers to every possible way of unpacking all the candies by successively opening and removing one accessible wrapping at a time (if several wrappings are accessible, in arbitrary order):
(1) There is exactly one wrapping which contains the whole parcel.
(2) On opening this and every further wrapping it turns out that its content consists either of at least three sub-parcels, all provided with a wrapping, or of exactly one unwrapped candy.
Determine the largest possible number of wrappings that such a parcel can have.

Determine all sequences of numbers $(a_n)$ with $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ which satisfy the following conditions (1), (2):
(1) For all integers $m, n$ with $n > m > 0$: $a_{n+m}\cdot a_{n-m} = a_n^2 - a_m^2$.
(2) $a_1 = 1$ and $a_2 = \frac52$.

Let $k_1, \dots, k_n$ be solid balls, each understood including its boundary points. These balls are placed arbitrarily in space; they are also allowed to penetrate or touch each other. Let the union of the $k_i$ have volume $V$. Prove that under these assumptions it is always possible to make a selection from the balls $k_i$ such that any two of the selected balls have no point in common and the union of the selected balls has a volume $U \ge \frac{1}{27}V$.
Determine the smallest positive integer $a$ for which $(a+1)^5 - a^5 - 1$ is divisible by $18305$.

Determine all those natural numbers $n \ge 3$ for which the following statement holds: every plane convex $n$-gonal region $A_1A_2\dots A_n$ is completely covered by the regions of the $n$ circles having the segments $A_iA_{i+1}$ as diameters ($i = 1, 2, \dots, n$; set $A_{n+1} = A_1$). Here every $n$-gonal region and every disk is understood including its boundary points.

(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. In a mathematics camp, a group leader proposes to the $n$ students ($n \ge 3$) of his group to choose the student who is to do the blackboard duty by the following method: the students are numbered $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$ and stand in a circle in this order, where (in the direction $P_1, P_2, \dots$) $P_n$ is again followed by $P_1$. First a coin toss decides whether $P_1$ or $P_2$ leaves the circle: if heads is up, $P_1$ leaves, if tails, $P_2$. Then the elimination is continued with those two students not yet eliminated who follow, in the stated direction, the student just eliminated last. On heads, again the first of these two in that direction leaves, on tails the second. This is repeated until only one student remains, who is then designated to be on duty.
(a) In the case $n = 3$, compute the probabilities $W_1$, $W_2$, $W_3$ that $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$, respectively, are designated to be on duty.
(b) Prove for every $n \ge 3$ that the selection method is unfair, i.e. that the probability of being designated to be on duty is not the same for all students $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_n$.
Remark: If some random event $A$ occurs as a consequence of any one of $m$ events out of a total of $N$ possible events (which are mutually exclusive and equally likely), then the number $p = \frac{m}{N}$ is called the probability of the event $A$.

Version B. Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{1987}$ be non-negative real numbers for which the sum of the squares equals $10$ and the sum of the cubes is greater than $1$. Investigate whether under these assumptions it is always possible to select
(a) $9$ of these numbers,
(b) $10$ of these numbers
such that the sum of the selected numbers is greater than $1$. (If a number occurs several times among $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{1987}$, it may be included among the selected numbers at most as often.)

In a plane, let $G$ be the set of all those points whose Cartesian coordinates are integers. Furthermore, let $F$ be a set of $1988$ different colors. Prove: for every distribution of colors in which each point of $G$ receives exactly one of the colors of $F$, there are in $G$ four points of the same color which are the vertices of a rectangle with sides parallel to the axes.

Determine all those triples $(x, y, z)$ of real numbers which satisfy the following system of equations (1), (2), (3):
$$\begin{aligned} 1\cdot x^3 + 9\cdot y^2 + 8\cdot y + 8 &= 1988, &(1)\\ 1\cdot y^3 + 9\cdot z^2 + 8\cdot z + 8 &= 1988, &(2)\\ 1\cdot z^3 + 9\cdot x^2 + 8\cdot x + 8 &= 1988. &(3) \end{aligned}$$

How many different words $(a_1a_2a_3\dots a_{n-1}a_n)$ can be formed in total from the letters $a_i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$, $i = 1, \dots, n$, such that
$$|a_j - a_{j+1}| = 1$$
for $j = 1, \dots, n-1$?

Through a convex $n$-gon $P_1P_2\dots P_n$ which has an incircle $c$, let a line $g$ be drawn which meets the side $P_nP_1$ at a point $M$ and a side $P_kP_{k+1}$ ($1 \le k < n$) at a point $N$. The line $g$ is drawn in such a way that it bisects both the perimeter and the area of the $n$-gon, i.e. that the following conditions (1) and (2) hold:
(1) The lengths of the polygonal lines $MP_1P_2\dots P_kN$ and $NP_{k+1}P_{k+2}\dots P_nM$ are equal.
(2) The areas of the polygons $MP_1P_2\dots P_kN$ and $NP_{k+1}P_{k+2}\dots P_nM$ are equal.
Prove that these assumptions always imply: the line $g$ passes through the center of the circle $c$.

Let $(x_n)$ be the sequence defined by
$$x_1 = 1, \qquad x_2 = 1, \qquad x_{n+1} = \frac{x_n + 1}{x_{n-1} + 4} \quad (n = 2, 3, 4, \dots).$$
Investigate whether this sequence is convergent and, if so, determine its limit.

(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Alfred and Bernd share $n$ apples by deciding, for each individual apple in turn, by a random decision (e.g. tossing a coin) who receives this apple. Such a distribution process is called favorable for Alfred if and only if Alfred, not only at the end but during the whole process, never has fewer apples in his possession than Bernd. The probability $w(n)$ that a distribution process is favorable for Alfred is the quotient obtained when the number of all distribution processes favorable for Alfred is divided by the number of all possible distribution processes.
(a) Determine $w(4)$.
(b) Determine $w(n)$ for arbitrary natural $n \ge 2$.

Version B. Prove: for every natural number $n \ge 2$ and for any $n$ functions $f_1, f_2, \dots, f_n$ defined on the interval $0 \le x \le 1$ there are real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ with $0 \le a_i \le 1$ ($i = 1, \dots, n$) for which
$$\left|a_1\cdot a_2\cdot\ldots\cdot a_n - \sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i(a_i)\right| \ge \frac12 - \frac{1}{2n}.$$

Determine all real solutions $(x, y, z)$ of the system of equations
$$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1, \qquad x + 2y + 3z = \sqrt{14}.$$

Investigate whether for every natural number $n \ge 1$ there is a function $f$ which satisfies the following conditions:
(1) The function $f$ is defined for all real numbers $x$.
(2) There is a real number $x$ with $f(x) \neq 0$.
(3) If functions $f_1, f_2, \dots, f_{n+1}$ are defined by the stipulations that for all real $x$
$$f_1(x) = f(x) \quad\text{and}\quad f_{k+1}(x) = f(f_k(x)) \quad \text{for } k = 1, 2, \dots, n,$$
then for all real $x$ the equation
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n} f_k(x) = f_{n+1}(x)$$
holds.

Determine all those convex polygons $P_1P_2\dots P_n$ in whose interior there exists a point $X$ for which $\overline{P_1X}^2 + \overline{P_2X}^2 + \dots + \overline{P_nX}^2$ equals twice the area of $P_1P_2\dots P_n$.

To open a safe, an unknown three-part combination $(a_1, a_2, a_3)$ must be set, where the three numbers can be set independently of one another and exactly $8$ values are possible for each of the three numbers. Due to a defect, however, the safe already opens whenever a set combination $(k_1, k_2, k_3)$ satisfies at least two of the three conditions $k_i = a_i$ ($i = 1, 2, 3$). Determine the smallest number $N$ for which there are $N$ combinations such that, on trying them out, the safe must open in every case (i.e. for every unknown combination $(a_1, a_2, a_3)$).

For a tetrahedron $ABCD$ it is assumed that the center $M$ of the circumsphere of the tetrahedron lies in the interior of the tetrahedron. The line joining $M$ with each of the vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ meets the face of the tetrahedron opposite to the respective vertex at $A'$, $B'$, $C'$, $D'$, respectively. Let the radius of the circumsphere be $r$. Prove that these assumptions always imply
$$\overline{AA'} + \overline{BB'} + \overline{CC'} + \overline{DD'} \ge \frac{16}{3}r.$$

(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Prove: for every natural number $n > 1$ and for any $n + 2$ real numbers $p, q, a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ which satisfy
$$0 < p \le a_i \le q \quad (i = 1, 2, \dots, n), \qquad (1)$$
the two inequalities
$$n^2 \le \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{a_k}\right) \le n^2 + \left[\frac{n^2}{4}\right]\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{p}{q}} - \sqrt{\frac{q}{p}}\right)^2 \qquad (2)$$
hold.
Note: For real $x$, as usual, $[x]$ denotes the integer $[x] = g$ with $g \le x < g + 1$.
Furthermore, for given $n, p, q$ with $0 < p \le q$, determine all those $a_i$ satisfying (1) for which in (2) equality holds
(a) between the first and the second number,
(b) between the second and the third number.

Version B. Determine the largest possible number of squares of side length $1$ which can be placed in a given square of side length $1.99$ without protruding beyond its boundary and without overlapping each other.

For every real number $a$, investigate whether the equation
$$\sqrt{a + \sqrt{a + \sqrt{a + \sqrt{x}}}} = x \qquad (1)$$
has (at least) one real solution $x$, and determine all real solutions of equation (1).

A piece of forest is bounded by a segment $CD$ (see figure). In the half-plane which is bounded by the line through $C$ and $D$ and in which the forest does not lie, on the line through $C$ perpendicular to $CD$, there is a hare at a point $A$ and a wolf at a point $B$ between $A$ and $C$. Here $\overline{AB} = \overline{BC} = a$ and $\overline{CD} = 5a$ with a given length $a$. The hare runs in a straight line with constant speed from the point $A$ to a target point $X$ of the segment $CD$ chosen by it. The wolf can run at most half as fast as the hare. The hare is caught by the wolf on the way if and only if the segment $AX$ contains a point $H$ which the wolf can reach at the same time as the hare or even earlier. Determine all those points $X$ on $CD$ whose choice as target point ensures that the hare is not caught by the wolf on the way.

Prove: for every system $(a, b, c, d)$ of positive integers $a, b, c, d$ satisfying the conditions $a\cdot b = c\cdot d$ and $a + b = c - d$, there is a right triangle whose side lengths, measured in cm, all have integer numerical values and whose area, measured in $\mathrm{cm}^2$, has the numerical value $a\cdot b$.

Determine all those triples $(x, y, z)$ of natural numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ which satisfy the following system of equations (1), (2):
$$\begin{aligned} x + 2y^2 - 3z &= 17, &(1)\\ x^2 - 3y + 2z &= 9. &(2) \end{aligned}$$

Let the vertices of a cube with given edge length $a$ be labeled $A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H$ as in the figure. Let $\varepsilon_1$ be the plane in which $A, B, C, D$ lie; let $\varepsilon_2$ be the plane in which $B, C, G, F$ lie; let $g$ be the line through $H$ and the center $M$ of the square $BCGF$. Prove that among all segments which connect a point of $\varepsilon_1$ with a point of $\varepsilon_2$ and whose midpoint lies on $g$, there is a segment of smallest length. Determine this smallest length.

(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Two urns $A$ and $B$ contain in total exactly $m$ red and exactly $n$ blue balls. The total number of balls is greater than $2$; at least one of the balls is red. At the beginning, $A$ contains all red and $B$ all blue balls. The balls are to be mixed by alternately taking, one after the other, a randomly selected ball from $A$ and from $B$ and putting it into the other urn. One begins with a removal from urn $A$. Determine all those pairs $(m; n)$ of numbers $m$ and $n$ for which the fourth ball moved is red with probability $\frac12$.
Note: If an urn contains exactly $Z$ balls, random selection of a ball here means that for all $Z$ balls the probability of being selected is $\frac{1}{Z}$. More generally, if of $M$ possible events $G$ are considered favorable and $M - G$ unfavorable, and all $M$ events are equally likely, then the probability of the occurrence of a favorable event is $\frac{G}{M}$.

Version B. For every natural number $n$ with $n > 1$, determine all those functions $f$ which, with this number $n$, satisfy the following conditions (1), (2), (3):
(1) The function $f$ is defined for all real numbers $x$.
(2) The function $f$ is continuous at the point $x = 0$.
(3) For every real number $x$: $n\cdot f(nx) = f(x) + nx$.

For every triple $(a, b, c)$ of positive real numbers $a, b, c$, determine all those triples $(x, y, z)$ of real numbers which satisfy the following system of equations (1), (2), (3):
(1) $x^2 - (y-z)^2 = a$,
(2) $y^2 - (z-x)^2 = b$,
(3) $z^2 - (x-y)^2 = c$.

For a cube-shaped box with edge length $10$ cm, consider all those lines, called marked, which pass through the interior of the cube, run parallel to an edge of the cube and have integer distances (measured in cm) from the two faces containing this edge. Prove: however the box is completely filled with $250$ rectangular building blocks of dimensions $2\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} \times 1\text{ cm}$, there are always at least $100$ marked lines which pierce none of the blocks. Here a block counts as pierced if and only if the line contains interior points of the block.

Determine all those functions $f$ which satisfy the following conditions (1) and (2):
(1) The function $f$ is defined and continuous for all real numbers $x$.
(2) For every real number $x$: $f(x) - 4f(x^2) = x - 16x^4$.

A strictly increasing sequence of numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ is called $m$-narrow if and only if the inequalities $x_a - x_{a-1} \le m$ hold for all $a = 2, \dots, n$. A set $A$ of numbers is called $m$-dense if and only if for every natural number $n \ge 2$ it contains an $n$-term strictly increasing sequence which is $m$-narrow. Prove the following statement (which weakens a famous theorem of the Dutch mathematician B. L. van der Waerden): for every partition of the set $N$ of all natural numbers into a number $r \ge 2$ of pairwise disjoint non-empty subsets $T_1, \dots, T_r$ there is a positive number $m$ such that (at least) one of the sets $T_1, \dots, T_r$ is an $m$-dense set.

Remark: Merely citing this theorem of van der Waerden (in which arithmetic sequences occur instead of $m$-narrow ones) as a known fact without proof would not suffice for a solution of this problem.

Determine a polynomial
$$f(x) = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + \dots + a_nx^n \quad (a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \text{ real}; \ a_n \neq 0) \qquad (1)$$
which satisfies the conditions
$$\begin{gathered} f(-4) = 0, \quad f(-3) = 1, \quad f(-2) = 0, \quad f(-1) = -1, \quad f(0) = 0, \\ f(1) = 1, \quad f(2) = 0, \quad f(3) = -1, \quad f(4) = 0 \end{gathered} \qquad (2)$$
and has the lowest possible degree $n$.

(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Prove: in every triangle $ABC$, for every point $P$ in the interior of the triangle, the lengths $x = PA$, $y = PB$, $z = PC$ and the lengths $u$, $v$ and $w$ of the perpendiculars dropped from $P$ to the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ (or their extensions), respectively, satisfy the inequality
$$xyz \ge (v+w)(w+u)(u+v).$$

Version B. For natural numbers $n, k$ with $2 \le k \le n$, a set $N$ of $n$ persons is called $k$-familiar if and only if in every set $K$ of $k$ persons from $N$ there is a person who is acquainted with all other persons of $K$. For every natural number $n \ge 2$, determine all those natural numbers $k$ with $2 \le k \le n$ for which the statement holds that every $k$-familiar set of $n$ persons must also be $n$-familiar.
Notes: For persons $a, b$ always: if $a$ is acquainted with $b$, then $b$ is acquainted with $a$. Furthermore it is assumed that every theoretically consistent distribution of mutual acquaintance or non-acquaintance in a set can also be realized by a set of persons.

On a circle $k$ let $A_1$, $A_2$ and $P$ be three pairwise distinct points; the segment $A_1A_2$ is not a diameter of $k$. For $i = 1, 2$, let $k_i$ be a circle which touches $k$ externally at $A_i$, and let $B_i$ be the intersection point, different from $A_i$, of the circle $k_i$ with the line through $P$ and $A_i$. Let the center of $k_i$ be $M_i$. Prove that under these assumptions the lines $a$, $b$, $m$ through $A_1, A_2$, through $B_1, B_2$ and through $M_1, M_2$, respectively, either all three have exactly one point in common or are all three parallel to each other.

Prove: if $p$ is a prime and two integers $n, k$ with $0 \le k \le n$ are written in the numeral system with base $p$ as
$$n = a_t\cdot p^t + a_{t-1}\cdot p^{t-1} + \dots + a_1p + a_0,$$
$$k = b_t\cdot p^t + b_{t-1}\cdot p^{t-1} + \dots + b_1p + b_0$$
($a_j, b_j$ integers with $0 \le a_j < p$, $0 \le b_j < p$ for $j = 0, 1, \dots, t$), then the number $\binom{n}{k}$ leaves on division by $p$ the same remainder as
$$\binom{a_t}{b_t}\cdot\binom{a_{t-1}}{b_{t-1}}\cdot\ldots\cdot\binom{a_1}{b_1}\cdot\binom{a_0}{b_0}.$$
Note: For integers $n \ge 0$ and $k \ge 1$, $\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n\cdot(n-1)\cdot\ldots\cdot(n-k+1)}{1\cdot 2\cdot\ldots\cdot k}$ is defined; furthermore, for integers $n \ge 0$, $\binom{n}{0} = 1$.

Let $P_1P_2P_3$ be a given arbitrary triangle; let its area be $F$, and let its incircle have center $M$ and radius $r$.
(a) Prove that a pyramid $P_1P_2P_3S$ has, among all pyramids $P_1P_2P_3S$ with this base $P_1P_2P_3$ and with given volume $V$, the smallest possible surface area if and only if the perpendicular from $S$ to the plane through $P_1, P_2, P_3$ has the foot $M$.
(b) Prove that this smallest possible surface area is $F + \sqrt{F^2 + \left(\frac{3V}{r}\right)^2}$.

Let $a$ be an arbitrary real number with $a \ge 2$. For $a$, determine all functions which satisfy the following conditions (1), (2), (3):
(1) The function $f$ is defined for all non-negative integers $x$; all function values $f(x)$ are real numbers.
(2) For all non-negative integers $x, y$ with $x \ge y$: $f(x)\cdot f(y) = f(x+y) + f(x-y)$.
(3) $f(1) = a$.
Remark: $f$ is to be given as an elementary function in closed form, i.e. the values $f(x)$ are to be given by a formula obtained by applying arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) to $x$ and to constants, power functions, exponential functions, trigonometric functions of $x$ or inverse functions of such functions, with a number of steps independent of $x$.

(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. Investigate whether there are a number $n \ge 2$, a positive real number $c$ and $n$ positive real numbers $a_i$ ($i = 1, 2, \dots, n$) such that the sum of the $a_i$ equals $n\cdot c$, the sum of the squares of the $a_i$ equals $2n\cdot c^2$, and at least one of the numbers $a_i$ is greater than $\left(1 + \sqrt{n-1}\right)\cdot c$.

Version B. A utopian novel tells of an author who lives infinitely long. Every day he writes a text with which he fills at least one sheet of paper and, if he starts further sheets on that day, also fills each of these sheets on the same day. In the course of each year he fills a number of sheets in this way; for different years these numbers may be different, but in no year does this number exceed $730$. Prove: in the life of this author, for every positive integer $n$ there is a period of consecutive days in which the author fills exactly $n$ sheets.
Note: It is assumed that the rule currently in force holds forever, according to which among any eight consecutive years there is always at least one leap year with $366$ days, while every non-leap year consists of $365$ days.

Of the vertices of a regular $250$-gon, exactly $16$ were colored yellow and all others blue. Prove that for every such coloring there is a rotation of the $250$-gon about its center which takes all yellow vertices to blue ones.
Prove that a cube can be dissected into exactly $n$ cubes for every natural number $n \ge 100$.

About $1993$ points $P_1, \dots, P_{1993}$ it is assumed that no three $P_i, P_j, P_k$ of them ($i 
eq j$, $i 
eq k$, $j 
eq k$) lie on a common line. Furthermore, for certain pairs $(i, j)$ with $1 \le i < j \le 1993$ the segment $P_iP_j$ has been constructed; it is assumed that each of the $1993$ points $P_i$ is connected with at least $1661$ other of these $1993$ points by one of the constructed segments. Prove that these assumptions always imply: among the $P_i$ there are $7$ points each of which is connected with each other of these $7$ points by one of the constructed segments.

Prove: if real numbers $a, b, c$ satisfy the system of equations
$$a + b + c = 2, \qquad ab + ac + bc = 1,$$
then
$$0 \le a \le \frac43, \qquad 0 \le b \le \frac43, \qquad 0 \le c \le \frac43.$$
Determine the largest possible number of triangles with integer side lengths and perimeter $1993$ among which no two are congruent to each other.

(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. A bus-train round trip through $n$ cities is a trip which starts in one of these cities, reaches each other one of them exactly once, then leads back to the starting point, and uses no means of transport other than bus or train. About $n$ cities $S_1, \dots, S_n$ it is assumed that between any two of them there is exactly one connection (usable in both directions), and that this is either only a bus connection or only a train connection. Prove for every natural number $n \ge 3$ that through $n$ cities satisfying these assumptions there must always be a bus-train round trip in which the means of transport is changed at most once.

Version B. A function $f$ satisfies the following assumptions: $f$ is defined and continuous for all real numbers $x$, all function values $f(x)$ are real numbers, and for every real $x$: $f(f(f(x))) = x$. Prove: these assumptions are satisfied only by the function $f$ defined for all real $x$ by $f(x) = x$.

For each of the two statements (a) and (b) below, investigate whether this statement is true for every set containing exactly $32$ positive integers, each of which is less than $112$ and no two of which are equal:
(a) There is a number which occurs at least five times among the differences of any two of these numbers.
(b) There is a number which occurs at least six times among the differences of any two of these numbers.
Note: In this problem the difference of two numbers $x, y$ is always understood to be the number $|x - y|$. If $x, y$ are numbers of a set mentioned above, this difference is counted only once among all differences to be considered (not twice, as $|x - y|$ and as $|y - x|$).

For $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ let
$$s_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac1k = 1 + \frac12 + \frac13 + \dots + \frac1n,$$
$$t_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k\cdot s_k^2} = \frac{1}{1\cdot s_1^2} + \frac{1}{2\cdot s_2^2} + \frac{1}{3\cdot s_3^2} + \dots + \frac{1}{n\cdot s_n^2}.$$
Prove the inequality $t_n < 2$ for all $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$

Let $ABCDS$ be a right four-sided pyramid with apex $S$ and square base $ABCD$. Furthermore, let $A', B', C', D'$ be four points lying on the lateral edges $AS$, $BS$, $CS$ and $DS$, respectively, at arbitrarily given (non-zero) distances $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$, respectively, from $S$. Show that under these assumptions the following always holds: the points $A', B', C', D'$ lie in a common plane if and only if
$$\frac1a + \frac1c = \frac1b + \frac1d.$$

For every triangle $ABC$, let $D$ and $E$ be the intersection points of the angle bisectors from $A$ and $B$ with the opposite sides $BC$ and $AC$, respectively; furthermore, let $P$ be an arbitrary point of the segment $DE$. Prove: under this assumption, the sum of the distances of the point $P$ from the lines through $B, C$ and through $A, C$ always equals the distance of the point $P$ from the line through $A, B$.

In Dwarfland live $12$ dwarfs. Each of them has an odd number of friends among the $11$ others; all these friendships are mutual. In each month one of the $12$ dwarfs has his birthday. Each dwarf lives alone in a house; each house is painted either red or green. Every year, on his birthday, each dwarf paints his house in the color which occurs more often than the other color among the colors of the houses of his friends. Show that under these assumptions there must always exist a moment from which on the color of all houses remains unchanged.

(This problem was set in two alternative versions A and B.)

Version A. For all positive integers $n$ define
$$f(n) = \left[2\sqrt{n}\right] - \left[\sqrt{n-1} + \sqrt{n+1}\right].$$
Determine all those positive integers $n$ for which
(a) $f(n) = 1$,
(b) $f(n) = 0$
holds.
Note: If $r$ is a real number, the integer $g$ for which $g \le r < g + 1$ is denoted by $g = [r]$.

Version B. Determine all those pairs $(m; n)$ of non-negative integers $m, n$ for which $2^m - 5^n = 7$.
